The Book of the Clouding Over had told us about those who are the “eyes of God,” without whom God would neither see the world nor be seen by it. Majnun's love makes him such a “divine eye.” The man who once gazed into the mirror has himself become the mirror in which God is contemplated, for his vision of Beauty was a vision of God contemplating himself. Ruzbihan could hardly have expressed more forcefully his understanding of human love as divine love. These are among the most astonishingly concentrated passages in the Jasmine.

Consider their claims carefully: among those faithful to love, vision is proportionate to the degree of love; the power to find depends on the heart. It is love that makes us see. The object we see is not what causes our love—one could scarcely express this more clearly in terms of the experience of perception itself. Love is the organ through which beauty is perceived. Where love is absent, beauty will never reveal itself.

But whoever possesses love—whoever is a Majnun—rediscovers the Eternal Witness of Contemplation here on earth. Speaking of himself, and wishing to dismiss the pitiful imitators of a way of life whose secret they do not understand, Ruzbihan will say elsewhere that it was by virtue of the Spirit's preexistent nature that “this audacious champion of tawhîd,” “this truly free man (âzâdeh),” rediscovered the secret of the uncreated within the created world itself.
But reaching that point requires the whole schooling of love, every stage of the inner pilgrimage.

The end of the chapter considered here announces that destination, anticipating the pilgrimage's end. When the mystic has become the eye through which God sees himself, the human shâhid, the beautiful human face, is seen by this divine eye.

But what God sees is his own face: that is precisely what his shâhid is. It is God who loves himself in Majnun's love for Layla. The human shâhid becomes the mashhûd, the Contemplated One, of the Eternal Witness. “When He makes him both the one who desires and the one desired, both lover and beloved, his servant in love assumes before Him the role of Witness of Contemplation (he is the shâhid-e Haqq). God contemplates himself in him with an eternal contemplation and clothes him in his own Attributes.

“Yet there is no incarnation, for the divine Essence remains apart from everything temporal.” That is why Ibn Arabi, interpreting the same theme of the “Am I not?” (A-lasto?) developed here by Ruzbihan, will say that in posing the question the divine Being was questioning himself. And that is also why the passage from human to divine love—the transformation of love that is not yet love in its true sense (majâzî) into true love (haqîqî)—is in no way the transfer of love from one object to another.

God is not distinguished as one object that would be love, lover, and beloved, alongside another object that would not. Rather, the unity of love, lover, and beloved is the mystery of divine love; that three-in-one is God himself. To say this is already to anticipate our final theme, the destination of the inner pilgrimage. Every chapter, every moment of the Jasmine, announces it, foreshadows it, and points the way toward it.

This is the most difficult theme in the Jasmine to analyze. Its elements are scattered throughout the book, as the preceding pages have shown. Nearly every statement of doctrine is accompanied by an autobiographical allusion, like a second melody sounding alongside the first. Then both melodies rise into a higher register and become an invocation to the beloved, always present in the mind, asking her not to fail in her role as shâhid. There are advances and returns, assertions and recollections, and aphorisms woven together. Anyone attempting an analysis can only mark out a few of the most important points along the way.
a) The Necessary Course of Love and Its Consequences (chapter XII)

“It happens in the course of time that love for the pre-eternal Beloved emerges into human love through a revelation of divine majesty (tajallî-e jalâl) shining through from the spiritual world. Ah! Do you not know what a book of wonders this story is? Once the divine eye (that is, the visible form of the Eternal Beloved) has been unveiled in the manifestation through which the divine appears, God shows himself to the mystics under the forms of created beings, in kindness and loving care.

“Thus, by way of created existence, the mystic is led into the very heart of the uncreated. For on the level of created things, it is from the dwelling place of created things that the journey must begin.” As Ruzbihan's anonymous commentator observes (Gloss 211): “The whole cycle of mystical experience (da’ira-ye ’irfân) is contained in this teaching.

“Through the self-revelation of the uncreated, the mystic contemplates the uncreated with the Spirit's inner sight; and at the very same time and in the very same place, he contemplates it in created forms of divine manifestation (majâlî-e hadath), with the eye that sees their outward, visible appearance.” And so, “although the Uncreated (through these manifestations in created things) leads them back to the Uncreated, the pilgrims on the path of love delight with childlike exuberance among the flowers of human beauty. For those flowers are the steps of the heaven of pre-eternity.

“Do not treat me cruelly, tender beauty, for in this incense burner the fragrant aloe of a particular divine manifestation burns before you, and the cup that is your pure soul holds the drink of intimacy with the Witness of Contemplation of the Uncreated. At this stage, this modest Sufi (Ruzbihan) is separated from pure tawhîd and suffers in the trial of your love ... You have become the qibla, the direction of prayer, of my soul ... Do not turn my soul into a world from which the Beloved is veiled, for the soul cannot remain deprived of the Beloved.

“Ever since the world of the soul (that is, the world before earthly existence), my soul has endured the pain of loving you. The soul that brought your soul into being is hidden within you, who are the soul of my soul. Tell me, what wonder is this that passes between these two ways of speaking?
At times the soul is the symbol of you, And at times you are the symbol of the soul. The soul is the earth on which you walk, And the earth on which you walk is the soul of my soul.”
b) Love as a School of Initiation (tarbiyat-e ’ishq, chapter XIII)

“The divine Being, in his eternal loving care, is neither inside nor outside the totality of created beings (neither immanent nor transcendent), yet he truly shows himself to their souls, or rather to the very eyes of their bodies. It is precisely by passing through the bounds of human existence that the Merciful One pours his grace upon the soul, so that the mode of being of the uncreated is perceived in a creature which, by comparison, is almost nonbeing.

“The dwelling place of imperishable love now becomes visible to them, because for a created being there is no road to the uncreated that begins in the uncreated. Some say, it is true, that such a road can be taken; but in reality a creature reaches divine love only through the teaching and initiation given by human love. There is one exception: a spiritual degree called the pure vision of the uncreated.

“But that dwelling place lies beyond the conditions of created existence. It was the rank of an elite among the prophets, the divine Messengers, and certain spiritual people ... Very few remain established in that spiritual state ... For most, their spiritual states come from the particular forms of divine manifestation suited to them, beginning, for example, with a manifestation in the form of human beauty.”

“The masters of mystical knowledge know that a created being has not the strength to endure the uncreated in its pure state. God's purpose is to begin by educating the disciple so that the laws of divine love may be revealed to him through human love. Then comes the succession of stages they describe, through which the soul must pass. Once kindled, the soul must experience fear of the beloved, then hope; then tears, groans, the tearing of clothes, exultation, crushing grief, passion, bewilderment, consolation, self-annihilation, speech, silence.

“All these states of lovers appear in those faithful to love. As they struggle with their own souls, they sound every one of these notes with the bow of tawhîd, when they attain that degree of mystical singleness which brings them face to face, alone, with their God. Everything that befell them at the beginning returns at this highest stage. They are great masters, and their knowledge carries authority.

“O my friend! How can I tell you that in the flowing waves of a lock of hair there trail the long streamers of inner revelations radiant as dawn? ... O wisest of all those who understand love! Wine from the Grail of pure Unity, poured into the cup where meanings mingle and overlap!

“The image of the two temples (ka’batayn) framed by curls, within the sacred precinct where one confronts the Face of Majesty ... Rise; lift up your right hand and display the majesty of love. For the muezzin's call announces that the hour of Prayer has come ... Enter the arena of my soul; and, like the rider's polo mallet striking the ball, let your love send my faith leaping from the ford of passing things to that high bank: We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit (Qur’an 2:83 and 254).”
c) The Descent of Love to Take Up Its Abode

One chapter (chapter XIV) returns, in the form of an autobiographical confidence addressed to the woman he loves, to the entire genesis of love: from the soul's preexistence to the moment when the four constituent elements analyzed earlier come together (chapter VI; see theme 3 above). “Then, with irresistible suddenness, this Sufi (Ruzbihan), cast out of the heavenly convent of pre-eternity, bursts into the streets of Shiraz. In mining the depths of unknown mystical knowledge, he has become, in the very school of the religion of the Law (sharî’at), a disciple of the religion of inner truth (haqîqat).”

What follows is a characteristic sequence in which images are not ornamental figures of speech but take the place of concepts, performing their work on a level beyond conceptual thought. The beautiful beings do not appear to the Sufi somewhere outside himself. They emerge from his most intimate secret—the very form of his destiny before time began. His bodily eyes merely serve the soul. Then comes the mystical birth of one faithful to love. His mother is none other than divine Beauty, which gives birth to him by revealing its mystery.

But Beauty must be assisted by a concrete form of beauty, the one corresponding to the lover's capacity established in pre-eternity. The place of this birth is the theophanic form issuing from the divine Act, the “mystical tavern” (compare Hafez), where one drinks from “the cup filled with the wine of double meaning.”

Hence these words: “(This Sufi) did not yet know that from the chamber of the most intimate secret of his own human reality there would emerge, draped in the veils of ambiguity, those beings of beauty in whom the divine Attributes take on personal form. He had to venture his head beyond the cloak of meditation; the eyes of his soul had to enlist his eyes of flesh in their service. Among visible forms, he watched for the distinguishing sign that would announce the Beloved.

“Suddenly, from the little street where the divine Act opens its mystical tavern, this maiden of the convent of Omnipotence emerged, covered by the great veil of her guarded chastity. Then she unveiled herself to the soul's gaze, which saw her without seeing her, for it saw her through the faculty of active imagination ... Is she not the midwife who helped bring him into the world, the mother of this earthly being, this Sufi who, following the traces of divine manifestations, burst into the street where Omnipotence unveils itself? ... And suddenly, repeating the Prophet Muhammad's words, he too declared: I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms.”

“Sometimes the lover's soul is among flowers, sometimes among laughter; sometimes burning with fire, sometimes trembling with music; sometimes the very substance of human clay is consumed by love's fire, and sometimes the lute of pre-eternity accompanies the sacred chant. Sometimes lost in inward intoxication, sometimes clear-minded, sometimes extinguished to itself. Sometimes in anguish, sometimes exulting; sometimes in fear, sometimes in hope; sometimes in separation, sometimes in reunion. In separation there is no station at which to rest; even in reunion there is no place to settle.

“All this is required of one faithful to love whom God leads through the stages of human love in this world toward the ascent of divine love, because it is one and the same love, and because it is in the book of human love that we must learn to read the law of divine love. This is the path of the Trial that initiates the faithful into pre-eternal love: they must follow the sweetness of human love along a path as narrow as a single hair, without falling into the depths of the hell of carnal nature.” Not to fall into that hell is to follow the example of the Prophet.

Through a ta’wîl, an interpretation that uncovers the inner sense of scripture, Ruzbihan finds this teaching in the Qur’anic account of the Prophet's great visions, in a way that beautifully illustrates the prophetic meaning he perceives in beauty. The Angel of Revelation descends upon the horizon: “He drew near, then hung suspended” (53:8). Addressing the beloved, Ruzbihan declares: “The scene in which this vision takes place is your very face, whose beauty overwhelms us with wonder.”

Yet the Qur’an also says of the Prophet: “His gaze neither swerved nor went beyond” (53:17). We already know the lesson Ruzbihan draws from this: one's gaze must neither “swerve” away from the vision of what the senses reveal, nor “go beyond” the image it presents, forgetting the image and seeing only the mirror—for that is how one falls into the hell of carnal obsession. He will return to this theme in another chapter which echoes his Book of the Clouding Over.

“When you have experienced love's ascent from (the stage expressed in this saying): Truly, I ask God's forgiveness seventy times each day—the fault of fixing your contemplation on the world of ambiguity while neglecting the Eternal Bride is forgiven through the power of this Sign: We have granted you a resounding victory so that God may forgive your former faults (48:2). Then you understand the hidden meaning of this verse: His gaze did not swerve, nor did it pass beyond the limit (53:17).”
Ruzbihan concludes, still addressing his beloved: “Perhaps you do not know how deep the heart's distress can be, or where the beloved dwells in relation to the soul.

“Open a page of my suffering and decipher there the letters of a mystical knowledge still unknown, so that you may understand how, in the presence of the visible form of the invisible, my love remains free from the troubling suggestions of carnal nature. What can I say? This story is the secret of the masters of mystical knowledge. They alone know its cipher, and in the anguish of what cannot be attained, they are the ones who can decipher its signs. There is a secret hidden from the concerns of ordinary people; and those who have revealed it have had their tongues cut out.”
d) Love's Journey Through the Heart of One Faithful to Love (chapter XV)

“Since the lights of Beauty have entered the mirror of the human face from the eye of God (the visible form of the Beloved), it is this human mirror that the human soul contemplates. In it, the soul discerns the particular divine Attributes in the manifestation meant for it (that is, in the form of beauty corresponding to its own capacity).

“Once the soul has discovered the secret of that capacity, it cannot help becoming intoxicated with love as it contemplates this Witness of Contemplation (shâhid) with the purity of sight appropriate to it. This story is the soul of the souls of the prophets; it feeds the souls of the spiritual Friends (Awliyâ’) and nourishes the soul of the Angel. At last it rules even the soul's innermost secret (sirr-e jân).

“The soul's essential reality (haqîqat) becomes one with love for the beloved. Through the triumphant power of the divine manifestation, the very soul of love becomes one with the soul of the beloved in the innermost depth of all (that is, the beloved becomes one with the love with which the lover himself becomes one). The soul of love floods the world of the soul with light, cleansing it of everything other than love. In a human being it replaces human conduct with the conduct of an Angel. From man's natural dispositions, love for the beloved removes all that is merely natural.”

“All this happens when, from the first beginnings of human love, the pilgrim is seeking divine love, and in the very human love that carries him away he travels in longing for the vision of God. Moment by moment, the soul of the soul, invited to the feast of this love by the invisible Eternal Bride, removes from love's secret the covering made necessary by the divine manifestation. Love itself then becomes the soul's protection.

“But if the soul clings to love's literal appearance, that attachment to the letter makes it a traitor to love; it will never reach love in its true sense (haqîqat, its divine reality). For whoever stakes everything on himself, remaining his own hostage, falls into a condition that leaves him unable to understand the human image of love and the beloved ... In the night when my heart was dispossessed, which wrapped me in a great veil, I offered an evening prayer in the little street of wandering.

“I spoke with the Angels of the soul of the feeling of absence experienced within the feeling of presence itself. Then, suddenly, amid the mourners of my secret anguish, I saw her who is the Venus of the heaven of mysteries become the harp of those who mourn. Come, let us see how the army of love's temptations behaves in the sanctuary of this beauty from Qipchaq; how, in the arena of a struggle that is both separation and attainment, those temptations are shattered in the vanguard of imagination by the army of her beauty.”
e) The Ascending Stages from Human Love to Divine Love (chapter XVI)

They are many; it would be an illusion to try to count them. The first, at any rate, is to acquire the necessary capacity. Next comes the awakening of the divine Attribute manifested in the theophany corresponding to that capacity. Then comes the inspiration that gives the first intimation of the deception or ambiguity of appearances (iltibâs). After that comes the light that makes it possible to see the archetype in the vision of a material form.

Then follow watching, waiting, undivided attention, fleeting glances, contemplation, vision ... Then the image is brought to life by active imagination (takhayyol-e khayâl); then the spiritual image (khayâl-e râhânî) is integrated into consciousness; then come consummation and the fire of love. Next, the feeling of having been robbed of everything; within that loss, searching; within that search, overwhelming passion. Temptations entering thought; astonishment that paralyzes the heart's subtle faculty of perception. Intimidation before the world of legalistic religion, a world with no insight into love.

Then comes the pursuit of passing inner states: terror at the prospect of perishing, desperate searching; the approach of the soul, the approach of the intellect, desolation of the heart; Abraham's laments, Moses' cries; fear without hope, hope without fear. There is the first great anguish; then the discovery of all-encompassing vision; complete intimacy, complete exultation; conversations in the night, private psalms, retreat, solitude. In the violence of what is undergone, one feels one's own annihilation; in the exquisite sweetness of what is tasted, one feels one's own abiding beyond annihilation.

“In the realm of human love's many qualities, each one, in thousands of possible forms, affects the lover's way of being, according to the figures produced by divine manifestations throughout the celestial cycle of the heavens that measure out the time of love. Once the lover has received the gift of a capacity for love, it is through the very perfection of human love that he reaches the beginnings of divine love. Then love, like an initiator, strips him of that first condition and lifts him, riding upon the divine manifestations, into the world of uncreated Majesty.

“From all eternity and for ever, he participates in the eternally enacted divine ceremony in the world of the Jabarût, in the company of those who dwell continually in the Malakût, the spiritual kingdom. That eternal contemplation is now his dwelling and his home ... So speaks this exile whose heart is in love (Ruzbihan). He states it plainly: love experienced for a human being is the ladder of love for the divine Being. This love is given to whom it is given; it is known by whoever knows it.

“And so, when I was walking beside the wall of the house of ambiguity, I saw this young beauty from Turkestan; her long eyelashes, like a volley of arrows, cut me off from everything that was not love. This inconsolable Sufi (Ruzbihan) speaks in such strange allusions that he misleads even the convent (khanqâh) of those intent on scrutinizing the mystery of Beauty. Do not imagine that this suffering has brought me any gain, or that this state of being confers any dignity upon me. This state resembles the chameleon of divine manifestations, each suited to its own occasion.

“Here, in the mirror of self-annihilation, the beauty that is abiding beyond annihilation must appear. Beware! Beware! For in this furnace Gabriel's wing, which is the soul, is consumed, and in the palace of servitude to love the garment of suffering is sewn. This young beauty thinks that this man (Ruzbihan) is the veil. She does not know that she herself is our veil. So be it: I call my suffering to witness.

“Or rather, no—it is neither this nor that. In truth, love has existed from all eternity. It needed only to enter the house of the desolate one night, for a single hour, and it made us one faithful to love. From then on, the soul had to advance step by step in the tracks of the mystery, beyond the heavens of becoming and passing away.”

Ruzbihan allows us to follow this ascent step by step. In a few magnificent lines he lets us witness the dawning of the lights of divine manifestation: “From the depths of the invisible, from the mystery of the divine manifestation, a Light among the Lights, one particular divine Attribute, begins to grow in the inner world of heart and soul.

“All the hidden figures shine through the veil of the manifestation, taking their places in the wide field where divine manifestations appear in their purity, in the meadow where lightning reveals the unseen reality of the divine Attribute. Each appears bearing the twofold mark of its origin: human and spiritual at once, material and yet alive. Each rightfully claims its proper place.

“Although in themselves these figures are mirages without independent reality, they take their stand in the shadow of the divine Attribute. Then the lights of divine self-revelation (anwâr-e tajallî) flood them, free of ambiguity, and give every one of them the savor of reality in its true sense (haqîqat). Those who have not yet attained the vision of divine manifestations are led by these figures to the very source of the light of manifestation (nûr-e tajallî).

“There, within true reality, they are led out of the stage of ever-changing diversity into the world of lasting establishment ... In sovereign power, the divine manifestation frees the soul of the soul, in its search for the beloved, from everything other than the beloved, everything belonging to the stage of ambiguity. It leads the Spirit breathed into man at the beginning out of its vessel of clay into knowledge of the divine Attributes that belong to it in its own right.”

Little by little, the image of the Eternal Bride (’arûs-e qidam) emerges and becomes more distinct. “The sovereign divine manifestation leads the bride who is the soul out of the recesses of human existence into the bridal chamber of divine intimacy. It clothes her in a robe woven from the lights of true Beauty.

“When the light of the divine Attribute makes itself felt by the consecrated soul, she sees nothing but the divine Being in the mirror of a being destined to pass away. For having passed through the first beginnings of human love, she has now reached the first beginnings of divine love.” This transition passes through three stages, corresponding to the three stages of tawhîd (see theme 6 below).

The first is simply the inclination of love experienced in the particular form proper to each being. At this stage, ambiguity has not yet appeared. It enters halfway along, at the second stage, when, for fear that the Spirits may yield to “longing for Paradise” (malah-e behesht), “Beauty reveals itself to them in the forms of divine manifestation, so that they may taste the peace of love in its divine Source.

“The third stage, the dwelling place of higher knowledge and tawhîd, is where the Spirit recovers its clear awareness (sahw) and loses itself (mahw).” Within that very self-effacement the Spirit once again discovers the secret of the uncreated hidden in the secret of what passes away.

But the old self has been burned away and annihilated, and perception is now entirely new: the lover knows that he himself is the beloved, and yet it is not himself that he loves. “He sees with the eyes of the innermost consciousness (sirr); beings that have received the gift of existence and must pass away taste peace at the murmuring of the doves of Uncreated Love.

“Otherwise how could he say: I contemplated my God in the most beautiful of forms?” “Up to this point,” Ruzbihan explains, “we have been speaking of the dwellings of the wandering stars in the heavens of the uncreated, as they travel among the constellations (abrâj) of the created world.”

“From now on, in the garden of tawhîd, the nightingales of mystical singleness (tafrîd) settle only on the branches of the rosebushes of freedom from material things (tajrîd). From the divine Being they receive the wine of the divine Attribute, tasted within that Attribute itself.

“Those acquainted with the highest teachings, pilgrims of the lights that reveal, know that these stages concern only pilgrims seeking the divine Being. They can say: the stages of divine love are explained by human love; for the grace of the young beauties of Turkestan is itself the tablet upon which the characters of an unknown writing must be deciphered. And it is from the battlements of the highest tower in the heaven of love that the wondrous Bride is glimpsed.”

Addressing the woman to whom his book is dedicated, Ruzbihan goes on: “Alas! If you understood what this means, you would draw aside the veil that conceals the human image of the one Eternal Bride. For the beauty of that image is the East in which rises the sun of Unity, a Unity bound to no particular form. Then this Sufi might secretly decipher, in the dwelling place of tawhîd, the writing of the divine Attribute between the intricate lines of the divine manifestation.

“Yet even now he reads, in the tresses of your amber-scented hair, radiant with the light of your beauty, this verse of the Book: You cause night to enter day, and you cause day to enter night (3:25).

“I know that the Spirit's reflection shines upon the face of this human icon. It is nothing less than the shadow of the divine Attribute, for the sovereign is God's shadow upon the earth. It is the hell of trial, rising in successive terraces; the wood that feeds the soul's fire; the ladder to eternal Paradise; the imprint of the seal: He shaped you—ah, how beautiful is the form he gave you! (40:66). There too the circle of the soul's horizon is arched.
“To it also refers the promise: We shall show them Our Signs (41:53). It is the influence of the stars of the uncreated East, for it bears the mark that prompts the cry: This is my God (6:76–78).”

In saying these things, Ruzbihan knows perfectly well the dangers and misunderstandings he is inviting. We have already heard him boldly profess malâmat, the willingness to bear other people's reproach. Here another opportunity for defiance presents itself: “I found acceptance among the mystics adorned with love.

“But to the pious devotees (zohhâd) my story is scandalous impiety. For those who steal into the palace of the Beloved, the color of reproach (rang-e malâmat) cast upon them covers the true face of their integrity. They keep the soul hidden in the soul's deepest recess. Outwardly they bear the mark of blame; but on the Preserved Tablet the letters of their names appear to the heavenly beings (malakûtiyân) in the reverse order from that in which earthly people read them.

“Within the inviolable boundary of their souls they possess the light of eternal blessedness, for the path along which their secrets (asrâr) advance is lit, in the deepest night of nonbeing, by the Uncreated Light. This is the fulfillment of the promise: God protects you against men (Qur’an 5:72).”

To have “reached the first beginnings of divine love” means that the passionate, commanding soul (nafs ammâra), brought under the Spirit's victorious authority, has become the soul at peace (nafs motma’yanna), the very soul addressed by the Qur’anic summons recalled at the beginning of this book. “Among the witnesses of contemplation (shawâhid) she has rediscovered the traces of that same Witness (shâhid). The purity of the divine Attributes has shone for her in the mirror of divine manifestation (âyînah-e fi’l).
“But she does not yet know which way lies the uncreated East, for she still dwells in the house of love's sorrows. The Joseph of true Reality has not yet risen for her out of the well of trial.

“When at last she leaves the prison of trial, she no longer finds quite the same sweetness in human love. She has tasted the traces of divine Beauty, whose subtle graces have freed her from the need for intermediaries. She has now reached the stage where, her education complete, she waits for the appearances of light ... From this point onward, love begins anew. From this stage the journey will lead to the furthest limit of love. Between these first beginnings and that final limit—I mean in divine love—there are twelve mystical stations.”

These are the twelve mystical stations described, one after another, in the final chapters of the Jasmine of the Faithful in Love (XXI–XXXII). Increasingly, the lived experience of love is expressed in the language of the problems raised by tawhîd. The journey is approaching its final destination: the secret of esoteric tawhîd, which cannot be discovered without experiencing love. It is precisely that experience which allows one to feel and to describe the relationship between divinity (lâhût) and humanity (nâsût) in terms of divine manifestation, without confusing it with incarnation.

For a theophany concerns the form of the body, not its material substance, its flesh. Ruzbihan's understanding of love, and of the implications of human and divine love for one another, is possible only where thought moves within a horizon of divine manifestations, transfiguring all flesh into caro spiritualis, spiritual flesh. It does not belong to a horizon defined by a historical incarnation, by an Incarnation of the divine in the human within History. We noted earlier how this distinction helps explain the affinity between Manichaeism and a mystical religion of love sustained by manifestations of the divine in beauty.

Finally, the characteristic point is that every question concerning the two aspects of one and the same Eros can be expressed in theological terms—more precisely, in the language of the esoteric wisdom of tawhîd—and the reverse is equally true.
We shall see a striking illustration of this before we finish.

At this point we can do little more than mark a few landmarks along the Way. Ruzbihan interprets the Qur’anic verse “God loves those who turn back to him” (2:222) as applying to those who “turn” to the religion of love. He wishes to invite those capable of seeing with more than the body's eyes to understand what that religion really is.

Yet this secret can be understood nowhere but among those faithful to love: “It is in the garden of love that the flowers of the Merciful One bloom.” For everywhere else, “whoever seeks divinity in humanity can only be, in view of the requirement to preserve God's transcendence (tanzîh), a scandalous unbeliever (kâfir).”

The light of tawhîd has remained ambiguous to them, and hundreds of thousands of souls still in bondage have failed to cross its threshold. When the Eternal Bride reveals herself, hell becomes paradise and the ascetic's cell becomes the Fire Temple. This guest from the heaven of pre-eternity (Ruzbihan himself) has contemplated pre-eternal Beauty through the veil—or mirror—of what passes away. Before divine Beauty, the veil hiding divinity was lifted.

Yet there are hundreds of thousands of cases in which the earthly beloved remains without a partner, while the whole universe of divine manifestations remains unknown, concealed within the majesty of the pure Essence.”

“Without a partner”: that is, without someone faithful to love, someone capable of recognizing a manifestation of divine Beauty in her beauty. At the same time, the entire universe of divine manifestations remains unknown. The majesty of the Essence remains in its transcendence. The threshold of tawhîd has not been crossed. In other words, the inner meaning of tawhîd has not even been suspected.
We shall see in the end what this correspondence means.

By contrast, “ecstatic experience (wajd) is dispossession, rapture, the Beloved’s secret cipher, the shock of sublimity, the onslaught of the pre-eternal world, the discovery of the wondrous realities of the Mystery. It is the irruption of the guards of the theophany, descending upon the Sinai of the Show Yourself to me (7:143) uttered by this new Moses, the soul.

“It is the crashing together of the waves of the Ocean of the uncreated; it is humanity’s innate capacity, the root of the universe; it is the vision of the forms shaped by the divine self-manifestations. It announces itself through an inwardly heard, personal summons; it breaks forth with the unveiling of the light of beauty. At that inward summons, in that transfiguration of being, the whole transient world offers the pure drink of ecstasy in countless cups. Ecstatic feeling has no limit, for existence itself has no limit.”

And then there is this invocation, spoken at the stage of certainty: “O image of beauty! Come to the aid of those who are beginners in love. For if mystics, troubled by the wound of the spear of ardent longing, look upon the witness of contemplation (shâhid) whom they behold in their gathering as though they were beholding the divinity itself, they are unbelievers, violating tawhîd, the oneness of God.

“But if I contemplate you while feeling the distance that separates me from the Inaccessible, then I am one of the faithful of love. Since this is so, I beg you, turn your gaze toward us, you who are the joy of the mystics, so that your gaze may lift us to the summit of pre-eternity.

“Love is the first fruit to ripen in its garden. I stand amazed; how could I not? For although the divine Attributes are present in these visible Signs (ayât), I know that tawhîd cannot admit incarnation (holûl). Is what I know of you, then, no more than presumption? If it is you whom I know, my knowledge amounts only to tashbîh—assimilating God to a creature.
“But if I know nothing of you, I reduce God to nothingness and abstraction (ta’til).”

Here the problem of love’s theophanic function—its power to reveal God—is stated with extraordinary precision. Tashbîh and ta’til are the two reefs on which abstract monotheism is forever in danger of running aground: making God too much like a creature, or stripping God of every living quality.

The theology of love demanded by the doctrine of theophany finds a passage between them. It cannot be confronted with a dilemma that arises only for the tawhîd of ordinary faith, because love is precisely what opens the way to esoteric tawhîd, an inward understanding of divine oneness. And only that understanding, in turn, can do justice to love’s paradox.

Islamic thought has steered between these two reefs with difficulty and varying success. Shiism in general, Ismailism, and the mystical philosophy of Sufism, however, have found a way through in the idea of theophany: the divine taking human form on the plane of the Malakût, the heavenly Pleroma or fullness of spiritual being. Rûzbehân has taught us enough about this heavenly manifestation in human form to show what it means. It is the mystery of the divinity revealing itself to itself; and, from the mystic’s side, this self-revelation is experienced and understood as the very mystery of love.

Here lies the origin of the relation between divine and human love, for there is only one and the same Eros. Human love must therefore be the indispensable initiation into divine love. To experience human love is to be initiated into the divine mystery, into the esoteric tawhîd professed by the “elect of the elect” among the mystics. This mystery is expressed as a seemingly paradoxical identity.

Our spiritual thinkers knew its Neoplatonic formulation well from the work known as the Theology of Aristotle. Rûzbehân gives it his own expression: “Before worlds existed, before there was any becoming of worlds, the Divine Being was itself love, lover, and beloved.” Or again: “Know that the Divine Being’s love is like its knowledge. It never ceases to be the lover of itself, just as it never ceases to know itself and contemplate itself through itself.”
This statement is paradoxical only to a religious or theological way of thinking that ends by turning the Divine into an object, pure and simple.

Indeed, a naïvely dogmatic consciousness accepts the statement only to begin reasoning boldly about God as though God were one object among others, distinguished from them by being a transcendent object—an object with that single exceptional property.
